subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 16-year-old boy has 2 months of progressive pain and swelling around his right knee. He is otherwise healthy with no known syndromes. Radiography shows a destructive metaphyseal lesion of the distal femur with periosteal new bone formation. He has no history of Paget disease or radiation exposure.
question: Which of the following best describes the epidemiology and typical location of the most likely primary bone tumor?

options.text: A malignant osteoid-producing tumor with peak incidence in males younger than 20 years, arising in the metaphysis around the knee
A malignant chondrocyte tumor with peak incidence in adults older than 50 years, arising in the medulla of the pelvis
A small blue cell tumor with t(11;22) arising in the diaphysis of the femur in young children
A locally aggressive benign epiphyseal tumor in women aged 20-40 years
A benign cartilaginous-capped metaphyseal outgrowth in males younger than 25 years

explanation_correct: Osteosarcoma accounts for about 20% of primary bone cancers and has its peak incidence in males younger than 20 years. It arises in the metaphysis of long bones, most often around the knee. Histologically it is characterized by pleomorphic malignant osteoblasts producing osteoid. Primary osteosarcoma in this age group is usually responsive to surgery and chemotherapy.

explanation_incorrect.B: That describes chondrosarcoma, which is most common in adults older than 50 years and arises in the medulla of the pelvis, proximal femur, or humerus.
explanation_incorrect.C: That describes Ewing sarcoma, which occurs in white males younger than 15 years and arises in the diaphysis, not the metaphysis.
explanation_incorrect.D: That describes giant cell tumor, a benign but locally aggressive epiphyseal lesion in adults aged 20-40 years.
explanation_incorrect.E: That describes osteochondroma, a benign metaphyseal projection with a cartilaginous cap that points away from the joint.

educationalObjective: Know that osteosarcoma peaks in males younger than 20 years and arises in the metaphysis around the knee.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 19-year-old man has a painful enlarging mass in his distal femur and recently sustained a fracture after minor trauma. Radiography demonstrates a malignant-appearing lesion with elevation of the periosteum forming a triangular density and radiating spicules of new bone. Biopsy shows pleomorphic cells producing osteoid.
question: Which of the following radiographic findings is characteristic of this tumor?

options.text: Onion-skin concentric periosteal reaction
Soap-bubble epiphyseal lucency
Small radiolucent nidus within the cortex
Codman triangle and sunburst pattern
Lytic lesion with intralesional calcifications

explanation_correct: Osteosarcoma produces malignant osteoid and can elevate the periosteum, producing Codman triangle, and form radiating spicules of new bone described as a sunburst pattern. It presents as a painful enlarging mass and may cause pathologic fracture. The tumor is aggressive, but primary disease in young patients generally responds to surgical resection and chemotherapy.

explanation_incorrect.A: Onion-skin periosteal reaction is characteristic of Ewing sarcoma, a small blue cell tumor of the diaphysis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Soap-bubble appearance is typical of giant cell tumor, a benign epiphyseal lesion.
explanation_incorrect.C: A small radiolucent nidus with night pain relieved by NSAIDs is osteoid osteoma.
explanation_incorrect.E: Lytic lesions with intralesional calcifications in older adults are characteristic of chondrosarcoma.

educationalObjective: Associate Codman triangle and sunburst periosteal reaction with osteosarcoma.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 68-year-old woman with long-standing Paget disease of bone develops new progressive pain and a mass in her proximal humerus. She has no prior radiation exposure or retinoblastoma history. Biopsy confirms a malignant osteoid-producing neoplasm. Her oncologist notes that this variant carries a worse prognosis than the classic form seen in adolescents.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's tumor?

options.text: A primary osteosarcoma in its typical age group with a good prognosis
A secondary osteosarcoma arising in a predisposed bone, with a poorer prognosis
A chondrosarcoma arising in the medulla of the humerus
A Ewing sarcoma with early metastases
A giant cell tumor with malignant transformation

explanation_correct: Osteosarcoma has a bimodal presentation: a primary peak in males younger than 20 years and a second peak in older adults, usually secondary to predisposing conditions such as Paget disease of bone, bone infarcts, prior radiation, familial retinoblastoma, or Li-Fraumeni syndrome. Secondary osteosarcomas, such as this one arising in Paget disease, have a poor prognosis compared with primary tumors in young patients. The tumor produces malignant osteoid and arises in the metaphysis of long bones.

explanation_incorrect.A: The classic primary osteosarcoma occurs in males younger than 20 years and is usually responsive to surgery and chemotherapy; this patient is older and has Paget disease.
explanation_incorrect.C: Chondrosarcoma produces malignant cartilage with intralesional calcifications, not osteoid, and is not specifically associated with Paget disease.
explanation_incorrect.D: Ewing sarcoma is a small blue cell tumor of children with t(11;22) and onion-skin periosteal reaction, not a Paget-associated osteoid-producing tumor.
explanation_incorrect.E: Giant cell tumor is a benign, locally aggressive epiphyseal lesion with osteoclast-like giant cells; it does not arise from Paget disease.

educationalObjective: Recognize secondary osteosarcoma in older adults with predisposing conditions such as Paget disease and its poorer prognosis.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 63-year-old man has several months of deep pelvic pain and a palpable mass. Radiography shows a large lytic lesion in the ilium with patchy intralesional calcifications and endosteal erosion. Biopsy shows malignant chondrocytes producing cartilage matrix. He has no history of radiation or Paget disease.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Osteosarcoma
Ewing sarcoma
Giant cell tumor
Osteochondroma with subsequent malignant transformation
Chondrosarcoma

explanation_correct: Chondrosarcoma is most common in adults older than 50 years and arises in the medulla of the pelvis, proximal femur, or proximal humerus. It is a tumor of malignant chondrocytes and typically appears as a lytic lesion with intralesional calcifications, endosteal erosion, and cortical breach. The pelvic location and cartilage-producing histology in this older patient are classic.

explanation_incorrect.A: Osteosarcoma produces osteoid, peaks in males younger than 20 years, and favors the metaphysis around the knee rather than the pelvic medulla.
explanation_incorrect.B: Ewing sarcoma occurs in white males younger than 15 years, arises in the diaphysis, and consists of small blue cells with t(11;22).
explanation_incorrect.C: Giant cell tumor is a benign epiphyseal lesion in adults aged 20-40 years with RANKL-positive mononuclear cells and a soap-bubble appearance.
explanation_incorrect.D: Malignant transformation of an osteochondroma does yield chondrosarcoma, but this patient has no known exostoses; this is a de novo chondrosarcoma.

educationalObjective: Identify chondrosarcoma as a cartilage-producing malignant tumor of older adults in the pelvis and proximal long bones.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 12-year-old white boy has 6 weeks of progressive pain and swelling in his left thigh with low-grade fever. Radiography shows a permeative lytic lesion in the diaphysis of the femur with concentric layers of periosteal new bone resembling onion skin. There is no history of syndromes.
question: Which of the following best describes this tumor?

options.text: A metaphyseal osteoid-producing tumor with sunburst spicules
A pelvic cartilage-producing tumor in adults older than 50 years
A diaphyseal small blue cell tumor of neuroectodermal origin in a boy younger than 15 years
An epiphyseal giant cell tumor with soap-bubble lucency
A cortical nidus causing NSAID-sensitive night pain

explanation_correct: Ewing sarcoma is most common in white patients, generally males younger than 15 years, and arises in the diaphysis of long bones, especially the femur, as well as pelvic flat bones. It is composed of anaplastic small blue cells of neuroectodermal or mesenchymal origin that resemble lymphocytes. The classic onion-skin periosteal reaction reflects layers of new bone formation. The tumor is aggressive with early metastases but is responsive to chemotherapy.

explanation_incorrect.A: That describes osteosarcoma, which arises in the metaphysis and produces osteoid with a sunburst or Codman triangle pattern.
explanation_incorrect.B: That describes chondrosarcoma, a malignant chondrocyte tumor of older adults in the pelvic medulla and proximal long bones.
explanation_incorrect.D: That describes giant cell tumor, a benign epiphyseal lesion in adults aged 20-40 years with osteoclast-like giant cells.
explanation_incorrect.E: That describes osteoid osteoma, a small cortical lesion with a radiolucent nidus and night pain relieved by NSAIDs.

educationalObjective: Recognize Ewing sarcoma as a diaphyseal small blue cell tumor of young white males with onion-skin periosteal reaction.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 13-year-old boy has a diaphyseal femoral mass. Biopsy shows sheets of anaplastic small blue cells that resemble lymphocytes. The pathologist notes that lymphoma and chronic osteomyelitis can look similar and orders a cytogenetic test that demonstrates a pathognomonic fusion transcript. The patient already has evidence of early pulmonary metastases.
question: Which of the following molecular findings confirms the diagnosis and best describes the tumor's behavior?

options.text: t(8;14) with MYC overexpression; indolent course
Germline TP53 mutation; multiple tumor types in the family
EXT1 mutation; multiple osteochondromas
t(11;22) producing EWS-FLI1; aggressive tumor with early metastases but chemotherapy responsiveness
Aneuploidy with no recurrent translocation; resistance to chemotherapy

explanation_correct: Ewing sarcoma is defined by t(11;22), which produces the EWS-FLI1 fusion protein; 11 plus 22 equals 33, referencing Patrick Ewing's jersey number. This translocation distinguishes it from other small blue cell lesions such as lymphoma and chronic osteomyelitis. The tumor is highly aggressive with early metastases, yet it is notably responsive to chemotherapy.

explanation_incorrect.A: t(8;14) involving MYC is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, not Ewing sarcoma, and Ewing sarcoma is not indolent.
explanation_incorrect.B: Germline TP53 mutation defines Li-Fraumeni syndrome, which predisposes to osteosarcoma and many cancers but is not the defining lesion of Ewing sarcoma.
explanation_incorrect.C: EXT1 or EXT2 mutations cause hereditary multiple exostoses and benign osteochondromas, with rare chondrosarcoma transformation.
explanation_incorrect.E: Ewing sarcoma has a specific recurrent translocation rather than only nonspecific aneuploidy, and it is chemotherapy-responsive despite early metastases.

educationalObjective: Associate Ewing sarcoma with t(11;22) EWS-FLI1, small blue cells, early metastases, and chemotherapy sensitivity.
